questions.stem: You are teaching Phoebe, 65, newly diagnosed with COPD in general practice, to use her salbutamol metered-dose inhaler with a small-volume spacer. She has shaken the inhaler and fitted it into the spacer. What should you tell her to do next?
options: Fire two puffs into the spacer together, then breathe in slowly through the mouthpiece
Seal your lips on the mouthpiece, fire one puff, then breathe normally four times
Fire one puff into the spacer, wait about 30 seconds, then take one deep breath in
Breathe in fast and hard through the mouthpiece while firing one puff into the spacer
questions.why: With a spacer, fire one puff at a time with the lips sealed, then either tidal-breathe about four times or take one slow deep breath and hold it for about 10 seconds. Shake the inhaler and repeat for each puff, and check technique at every visit.
notes: Firing several puffs at once makes the aerosol clump and stick to the spacer walls, so less drug gets to the lungs.
Waiting before inhaling lets the aerosol settle out on the spacer walls, so she should breathe in straight after firing.
A fast, forceful breath is the technique for a dry powder inhaler. With a spacer, slow or tidal breathing gets the most drug into the lungs.

questions.stem: Phoebe, 65, has moderate COPD (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50, FEV1 58% predicted) with breathlessness that stops her daily walks. Her blood eosinophils are 0.20 × 10^9/L. You have prescribed salbutamol as needed via a spacer. Which regular maintenance treatment should you start now in general practice?
options: Fluticasone propionate inhaler on its own, twice daily
questions.why: COPD-X recommends a long-acting bronchodilator, usually a LAMA such as tiotropium, when breathlessness persists despite a reliever. Step up to LAMA/LABA if she stays breathless, and add an inhaled corticosteroid only for repeated flare-ups.
notes: An inhaled corticosteroid on its own is not recommended in COPD. It raises the risk of pneumonia and does not give the bronchodilation she needs.
Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist used in asthma and has no established role in COPD.
Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index and many interactions, and is kept for later when inhaled therapy is not enough.

questions.stem: Phoebe, 65, a current smoker with 50 pack-years, has a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC of 0.50 with no significant bronchodilator response. Her chest X-ray shows hyperinflation, flattened hemidiaphragms and upper zone hyperlucency. What mechanism best explains the air trapping in her emphysema?
options: Reduced lung compliance stops the lungs emptying fully at end expiration, so gas stays
Reversible bronchial smooth muscle spasm narrows the large central airways
Loss of elastic recoil removes radial traction, so small airways collapse on expiry
Surfactant deficiency causes alveolar collapse that traps gas behind it
questions.why: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, which reduces elastic recoil (the force that drives expiration) and removes the tethering that holds small airways open. The airways collapse early in expiration and trap air. Compliance is increased, not reduced.
notes: Emphysema increases lung compliance. Reduced compliance is the restrictive picture seen in pulmonary fibrosis.
A reversible spasm would give a significant bronchodilator response, and her FEV1 rose by only 60 mL (5%).
Surfactant deficiency causes alveolar collapse with low lung volumes, as in neonatal respiratory distress, not hyperinflation.

questions.stem: You start Phoebe, 65, with moderate COPD, on an inhaled long-acting muscarinic antagonist. It works by blocking the acetylcholine that drives resting bronchomotor tone, the main reversible part of airway narrowing in COPD. The postganglionic fibres releasing this acetylcholine come from preganglionic fibres carried in which nerve?
questions.why: Parasympathetic supply to the bronchi runs in the vagus nerve (CN X) to the pulmonary plexus. Postganglionic fibres release acetylcholine onto M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle and glands, causing bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion, and this is what LAMAs block.
notes: The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) is motor to the diaphragm and does not supply bronchial smooth muscle.
The intercostal nerves are somatic nerves to the chest wall muscles and skin, not autonomic nerves to the airways.
Sympathetic fibres from T1 to T4 cause bronchodilation, and they are not cholinergic, so a LAMA does not act on them.
